summary: This RFC reviews proposals for letting one Internet network number stand for a group of physical networks under common administration. This hides internal complexity from the rest of the Internet and describes another subnet addressing scheme.

plainLanguage.summary: Outsiders see one address for a group of small networks, while inside the group a different method sorts out where things go.

questions: how can one network number cover several physical networks
subtitle: A subnet scheme using a fixed bit to distinguish internal subnets from the main network.

tldr.problem: Networks needed a practical subnetting scheme that hosts could implement, but proposals disagreed on whether the subnet field width should be fixed or variable, and how many subnets were needed.
tldr.mechanism: Reserve a fixed high-order bit of the host field to mark subnets; if set, use the rest of the high byte as a subnet number. For Class A and Class B networks, this allows up to 127 subnets. Hosts use a modified address interpretation for local addresses only.
tldr.outcome: UC Berkeley implemented this scheme successfully in 1984, proving it workable. However, it was superseded by variable-length subnet masks, which offered more flexibility and became the Internet standard.

today: RFC 936 documents a working subnetting scheme used at UC Berkeley in the mid-1980s. The Internet adopted variable-length subnet masks (RFC 950 and later CIDR) as the standard, which provides unlimited flexibility and is used by all networks today.

sections.title: Three Competing Proposals
sections.content:
By early 1985, three different RFC proposals existed for subnetting. RFC 917 (Mogul) suggested variable-length subnet fields encoded in the host address, requiring hosts to be modified. RFC 932 (Clark) proposed Class B 1/2 addresses that required no host changes but all router changes. RFC 936 (Karels, UC Berkeley) offered a fixed-bit approach: use a single high-order bit to indicate whether an address is a subnet, and a fixed 8-bit field for the subnet number.

Each scheme made different trade-offs between host compatibility, router requirements, subnet capacity, and implementation complexity. Berkeley chose RFC 936's approach because all their packet forwarding was done by hosts running the same OS, making host modification feasible.
sections.plainLanguage: Three teams had different ideas for splitting up a network. This one used a simple flag and fixed-size labels.

sections.title: The Addressing and Routing Logic
sections.content:
In the Berkeley scheme, hosts examine the high-order bit of the host field. If the bit is zero, the address is interpreted normally. If set, the remaining bits of the high byte are the subnet number. For a Class A network with 8 bits, this yields up to 127 subnets with 65,535 hosts each. Class B networks get up to 127 subnets of 255 hosts each.

Importantly, subnets are invisible outside the network. External routers never see or manage individual subnet numbers; they see only the base network number. Hosts treat subnet numbers as an extension of the network field, making subnets appear as independent networks internally while appearing as a single network to the outside world.
sections.plainLanguage: Inside the building, you can write '3rd floor' on your address. Outside, the building's one address is all anyone needs.

sections.title: Trade-offs Against Alternatives
sections.content:
Compared to RFC 932 (Class B 1/2), RFC 936 allowed more subnets within the space of a single network class. Compared to RFC 917's variable mask, it simplified implementation by fixing the subnet field width at boot time, avoiding complex dynamic discovery logic.

The drawback was that 127 subnets was still a hard limit for Class A or B networks, and the high-order bit constraint meant hosts could not use half the host address space. Despite these limits, the scheme proved workable in practice. However, CIDR (variable-length subnet masks) eventually became the standard because it offered greater flexibility across all address classes.
sections.plainLanguage: The idea worked well at Berkeley, but a simpler, more flexible method (CIDR) eventually won out globally because it adapted better as networks grew.
